text.p: If it were not for the green surgical hats, aprons, gloves and masks you might be tempted to think this was a video game in an amusement arcade rather than the operating theatre in a Belgian hospital.

At the Blasius hospital in Dendermonde, northwest of Brussels, doctors have this week been trying out an advanced form of keyhole, or minimally invasive, surgery -- one which puts a computer between the surgeon and his scalpel.
The space-age technique being tested -- dubbed telesurgery -- enhances a surgeon's movements by, for example, removing trembling, doctor Frederick Moll told Reuters in an interview.

Through inch-long slits in the patient's belly two metre-long mechanical arms, covered in plastic, gently manoeuvre until they reach their target -- gallstones in this operation -- guided there by a surgeon sitting with his back to the patient and watching a video screen.
He gets his picture from a tiny camera inserted through a third inch-long slit and steers the black, spider-like arms with joystick-like devices.

Unlike 'ordinary' keyhole surgery, the telesurgery tools allow for more precise movements while enabling the surgeon to reach parts inside the body hard to get to because they are in tight corners or very small.

Telesurgery screen pictures can be made bigger or smaller while information transmitted by a sensor built into the tips of the operating arms gives the surgeon's fingertips the feelings which they would get if they were actually inside the patient.
"With (regular) keyhole surgery you can't feel. You are also using rigid tools," said doctor Jacques Himpens of the Blasius hospital, who used the technology on some of his patients.
Moll said he brought telesurgery to Belgium for testing "because there is less bureaucracy, less paperwork."
In the U.S. regulators still have to approve the technique, pioneered at the Stanford Research Institute.
"We will continue to test and refine telesurgery," he said. "This is the new age of surgery...potentially we will be able to operate at a remote distance."

Moll, also medical director of California-based company Intuitive Surgical which developed the technique, said he was pleased with the results of the tests, which showed a much wider range of operations could be performed.
Just over a year ago, another Belgian hospital was involved in ground-breaking, long-distance surgery.

Using a joystick and a video screen, a surgeon in the St Lucas hospital controlled a robotic arm with a scalpel cutting into the abdomen of a man hospitalised in Utrecht, the Netherlands, before a camera was inserted to make a diagnosis.
